slides.title: Is your Core Customer still right?
slides.support: In Metronome: open War Room. Read your Core Customer aloud. Is this still the customer you most want more of?
notes: Put the team’s own Core Customer on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
In the example the company promises to have a customer live in 5 days today. Its differentiator, Live in a Day, is where that promise goes in 3 years.
Ask: are their three needs still right, in the same order? What did the year teach you about them?
Choosing one Core Customer and ranking their three needs was the Q2 work. If it is missing, keep going and mark the result draft.
Change only what the evidence changes. The differentiators must serve these needs.
slides.headline: Is your Core Customer still right?

artwork.alt: An example Core Customer for the subscription company. Core Customer: owner of a small business. Description: the owner of a business with 10 to 50 staff. They decide alone, pay by card, and want it working this month without an IT person. Prioritized needs. 1, up and running in days. 2, a cost they can predict. 3, a person to call when stuck. Prioritized benefits. 1, live in 5 days or fewer. 2, one flat monthly price. 3, a named contact for 90 days. Persona: Dana, owner of a 20-person business. Revenue 55%, profit 60%.

slides.title: Does your 3HAG line give you enough white space?
slides.support: In Metronome: open War Room. Put your Attribution Map on the screen. Is there enough white between you and your best competitor?
notes: Put the team’s own Attribution Map on the screen. The example here shows how to read it.
Say what the line is for. It gives the company white space, so it does not compete head on. It makes the company unique and valuable.
The dashed line is the best competitor score on each attribute. The white is the gap between it and the 3HAG line.
Point to both sides. On the left the company invests to lead. On the right it gives things up, and it will not compete there.
White space takes investment, and the company does not have unlimited funds. What it gives up pays for what it invests in. It does not overextend.
Where the two lines touch, the company competes head on.
Ask what has changed since the team drew the line at Q3. Agree on the line now, for the new 3-year date.
At the first annual this is a review. From the second annual on, rebuild the map from scratch: attributes, scores and line.
If the line is not agreed or the competitors are not scored, keep going and mark the result draft.
Close with the question that opens the next step: what must we do to create this white space?
slides.headline: Does your 3HAG line give you enough white space?

artwork.alt: A line graph for the example subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. A green 3HAG line and a dashed Best competitor line cross the chart. The space between them is white on a gray ground. On the left the 3HAG line is above the competitor line, at 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. That white is marked Invest. On the right the 3HAG line drops below it, to 2 on reporting and 1 on customization. That white is marked Give up. Where the two lines touch, on ease of use and reliability, there is no white. A faint line shows Us today.
